The Ocean’s Whisper

In the quiet between heartbeats, the sea speaks in a language older than words. It is not the roar of waves against cliffs that carries its truth, but the hush of water retreating over sand, the sigh of foam dissolving into itself. The ocean does not demand attention; it simply is—vast, indifferent, and endlessly patient.

I remember standing on a shore at dusk, the horizon a smudge of violet and gold, the sky bleeding into the water as if the two had forgotten they were ever separate. The wind carried the scent of salt and something else—something ancient, like the memory of the first rain. And in that moment, I understood: we are not visitors here. We are temporary shapes the earth has taken, like the dunes shifted by the tide.

The sea teaches without lessons. It does not scold the rock for standing in its way; it simply wears it down, grain by grain, until the stone forgets it was ever rigid. It does not mourn the fish that slip through its currents; it cradles their bones like secrets. And when the storm comes, it does not apologize for its fury—it is only doing what storms do: reminding us that stillness is just a pause between movements.

Some say the ocean is empty, but I think it is full—of lost ships, of whispered prayers, of the echoes of every tear ever cried. It holds the weight of time like a lover’s hand, pressing gently against the small of the back, urging us forward.

And what of us? We build our cities on its edges, as if proximity to its vastness will make us vast, too. We fill our pockets with its shells, as if owning a piece of it will make us less afraid. But the ocean does not care for our fear. It only asks that we listen.

One day, when the last human footprint has washed away, the sea will still be there, licking at the shores, indifferent and eternal. And perhaps that is its greatest gift: the quiet certainty that some things endure, while others—like us—are beautiful precisely because we do not.
